77869.q: Which seafarer do these emojis mean?
77869.e: Three ships, America and the famous “egg of Columbus” lead to Christopher Columbus. In 1492 he reached America with three ships.

77870.q: Which traveller do these pictures mean?
77870.e: A compass, camels and a route to China show Marco Polo. The Venetian travelled overland as far as China in the 13th century.
77870.m: Marco Polo travelled all the way to China in the Middle Ages.

77871.q: Whose expedition do these emojis mean?
77871.e: A ship, the Earth and a circle show the first voyage around the world. It began in 1519 under Ferdinand Magellan, who himself died on the way.
77871.m: The first voyage around the world began in 1519 under Magellan.

77872.q: Which seafarer do these pictures mean?
77872.e: A ship, spices and elephants point to India. In 1498, Vasco da Gama found the sea route from Europe around Africa to India.
77872.m: Vasco da Gama found the sea route to India in 1498.

77873.q: Which explorer do these emojis mean?
77873.e: Ice, penguins and a chequered flag show reaching the South Pole. Roald Amundsen was the first to get there, on 14 December 1911.
77873.m: Roald Amundsen was the first to reach the South Pole, in 1911.

77874.q: Which mountaineer do these pictures mean?
77874.e: A mountain, footprints and the summit show the first ascent of Mount Everest. Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first to stand on top, in 1953.
77874.m: Hillary and Tenzing were the first to climb Mount Everest, in 1953.

77875.q: Which seafarer do these emojis mean?
77875.e: A kangaroo, a ship and a map show the exploration of Australia. In 1770, James Cook mapped the east coast of Australia.
77875.m: James Cook explored the east coast of Australia in 1770.

77876.q: Which scientist do these pictures mean?
77876.e: Giant tortoises, islands and finches point to the Galápagos Islands. Charles Darwin visited them in 1835 and later developed his theory of evolution.
77876.m: Charles Darwin did research on the Galápagos Islands.

77877.q: Which Swiss adventurer do these emojis mean?
77877.e: A balloon circling the Earth shows the first non-stop balloon flight around the world. Bertrand Piccard achieved it in 1999 together with Brian Jones.
77877.m: Bertrand Piccard flew around the Earth in a balloon in 1999.

77878.q: Which invention do these pictures mean?
77878.e: A lamp with a plug in the house shows the electric light bulb. Thomas Edison made it practical for everyday use around 1880.
77878.m: Thomas Edison made the light bulb practical for everyday use.

77879.q: Which invention by Johannes Gutenberg do these emojis show?
77879.e: Books, a printing machine and letters show printing with movable type. Gutenberg invented it around 1450 in Mainz.
77879.m: Gutenberg invented printing with movable type around 1450.

77880.q: Which inventor do these pictures mean?
77880.e: A bell, and the telephone, belong to Alexander Graham Bell. He received a patent for the telephone in 1876.
77880.m: Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone in 1876.

77881.q: Which invention by Carl Benz do these emojis show?
77881.e: An engine, a vehicle and fuel show the motor car. In 1886, Carl Benz built the first motor car with a petrol engine.
77881.m: Carl Benz built the first car with a petrol engine in 1886.

77882.q: Which inventors do these pictures mean?
77882.e: Two brothers and an aeroplane show the Wright brothers. In 1903 they made the first controlled powered flight.
77882.m: The Wright brothers were the first to fly a powered aeroplane, in 1903.

77883.q: Which invention by Alessandro Volta do these emojis mean?
77883.e: Electric current from a store shows the battery. Around 1800, Alessandro Volta built the first battery, the voltaic pile.
77883.m: Alessandro Volta built the first battery around 1800.

77884.q: Which Swiss invention do these pictures mean?
77884.e: Burrs from plants got stuck to a dog's fur and to trousers. This gave the Swiss George de Mestral the idea for Velcro.
77884.m: Velcro was invented by a Swiss man.

77885.q: Which invention from CERN in Geneva do these emojis show?
77885.e: The world, a computer and links show the World Wide Web. Tim Berners-Lee developed it in 1989 at CERN in Geneva.
77885.m: The World Wide Web was invented at CERN in Geneva.

77886.q: Which invention do these pictures mean?
77886.e: A magnet and the points of the compass show the compass. Its needle is magnetic and points north; it was invented in China.
77886.m: The magnetic needle of a compass points north.

77887.q: Which machine of the Industrial Revolution do these emojis show?
77887.e: Rising steam, cogs and a factory show the steam engine. From 1769, James Watt improved it greatly.
77887.m: The steam engine powered the first factories.

77888.q: Which famous industry of eastern Switzerland do these emojis show?
77888.e: Thread, flower patterns and a factory show embroidery. Around 1910, St Gallen embroidery was Switzerland's most important export.

77889.q: Which machine of the textile industry do these pictures mean?
77889.e: Yarn and machine make spinning machine. It spun yarn much faster than a person at a spinning wheel.
77889.m: The spinning machine made spinning yarn much faster.

77890.q: Which problem of the Industrial Revolution do these emojis show?
77890.e: A child in a factory with long working hours shows child labour. The Swiss Factory Act of 1877 banned factory work for children under 14.
77890.m: The Factory Act of 1877 banned child labour in Swiss factories.

77891.q: Which industry of the Industrial Revolution is meant?
77891.e: A pickaxe, black rock and a shaft show coal mining. Coal was the most important fuel for steam engines.
77891.m: Coal was the most important fuel of the Industrial Revolution.

77892.q: Which development of the Industrial Revolution do these pictures show?
77892.e: Many people moved from the countryside to the towns to work in factories. This development is called urbanisation.
77892.m: During the Industrial Revolution, towns grew a lot.

77893.q: What was the first railway running entirely in Switzerland, which these emojis point to, called?
77893.e: Train and bread lead to the Spanish Bun Railway (Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn), which ran between Zurich and Baden from 1847. It was the first line entirely on Swiss soil and is said to have brought fresh pastries from Baden, the “Spanischbrötli”, to Zurich.
77893.m: The first railway line entirely in Switzerland ran from Zurich to Baden in 1847.

77894.q: Which way of producing things by Henry Ford do these pictures show?
77894.e: Cars, machines and a constant cycle show the assembly line. Henry Ford introduced it in 1913, and cars became much cheaper.
77894.m: From 1913, Henry Ford built cars on an assembly line.

77895.e: A rocket, the Moon and the first footprint lead to Neil Armstrong. In July 1969 he became the first person to step onto the Moon.
77895.m: Neil Armstrong was the first person on the Moon.

77896.q: What was the rocket that these pictures point to called?
77896.e: Rocket, the planet Saturn and the number 5 make Saturn V. This rocket took the Apollo astronauts to the Moon.
77896.m: The Saturn V took the astronauts to the Moon.

77897.q: What was the lunar module that these emojis point to called?
77897.e: An eagle on the Moon stands for the lunar module Eagle. Armstrong and Aldrin landed on the Moon in it in 1969.
77897.m: The lunar module of Apollo 11 was called Eagle.

77898.q: Which astronaut do these pictures mean?
77898.e: An astronaut, the number 2 and the Moon lead to Buzz Aldrin. Shortly after Armstrong, he became the second person to step onto the Moon.
77898.m: Buzz Aldrin was the second person on the Moon.

77899.q: Which Apollo 11 astronaut do these emojis mean?
77899.e: An astronaut circling the Moon in a spacecraft is Michael Collins. He stayed in the command module Columbia while the other two landed.
77899.m: Michael Collins orbited the Moon while his colleagues landed.

77900.q: Which mission do these pictures mean?
77900.e: A rocket and the number 11 show Apollo 11. On this mission in 1969, people landed on the Moon for the first time.
77900.m: Apollo 11 took the first people to the Moon in 1969.

77901.q: Which Swiss experiment on the Moon do these emojis show?
77901.e: Sun, wind and a sheet on the Moon show the solar wind sail of the University of Bern. It caught particles of the solar wind and was even set up before the US flag.
77901.m: In 1969, an experiment from the University of Bern stood on the Moon.

77902.q: Which famous sentence about the Moon landing do these pictures mean?
a: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind
77902.e: A small step, a giant leap and the whole world make Armstrong's famous sentence. He said it as he took his first step onto the Moon.
77902.m: Armstrong spoke of a small step and a giant leap.

77903.q: Which event in Swiss history do these emojis show?
77903.e: Three men raising their hands to swear an oath in a meadow show the Rütli Oath. According to legend, men from Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden swore on the Rütli to help each other.
77903.m: The Rütli Oath is an important legend about the founding of Switzerland.

77904.q: Which document of Swiss history do these pictures mean?
77904.e: A charter and the year 1291 show the Federal Charter. In it, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promised to help each other; it is kept in the Museum of the Swiss Charters of Confederation in Schwyz.
77904.m: The Federal Charter of 1291 is seen as the founding document of Switzerland.

77905.q: Which Swiss person do these emojis mean?
77905.e: A red cross, an ambulance and a prize lead to Henri Dunant. He started the founding of the Red Cross in Geneva in 1863 and in 1901 was one of the first to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
77905.m: Henri Dunant founded the Red Cross.

77906.q: Which right from Swiss history do these pictures show?
77906.e: A woman, a ballot box and a yes show women's right to vote. At national level, women in Switzerland have only been allowed to vote and elect since 1971.
77906.m: Since 1971, Swiss women have been able to vote and elect at national level.

77907.q: Which movement, led by Zwingli in Zurich, do these emojis show?
77907.e: The Bible, a church and renewal show the Reformation. Huldrych Zwingli started it in Zurich from 1519.
77907.m: Huldrych Zwingli brought the Reformation to Zurich.

77908.q: Which document from 1848 do these pictures mean?
77908.e: A legal text, the scales of justice and a government building show the Federal Constitution. With it, Switzerland became a federal state in 1848.
77908.m: Since the Federal Constitution of 1848, Switzerland has been a federal state.

77909.q: Which Swiss troop do these emojis mean?
77909.e: A guard at a church and a palace shows the Pontifical Swiss Guard. It has guarded the Pope in the Vatican since 1506.
77909.m: The Swiss Guard has protected the Pope since 1506.

77910.q: Which Swiss educator do these pictures mean?
77910.e: A teacher, a child, books and a heart lead to Pestalozzi. He worked for the education of poor children and wanted to develop “head, heart and hand”.
77910.m: Pestalozzi wanted to develop children's head, heart and hand.

77911.q: Which mountain railway, opened in 1912, do these emojis mean?
77911.e: A train, a young girl and a mountain make the Jungfrau Railway, because Jungfrau means maiden. Since 1912 it has run up to the Jungfraujoch, the highest railway station in Europe.
77911.m: The Jungfrau Railway has run up to the Jungfraujoch since 1912.

77912.q: Which job from the past do these emojis mean?
77912.e: In the evening, the street lamps were lit with fire and a ladder. That was the job of the lamplighter, before there was electric light.
77912.m: In the past, lamplighters lit the street lamps every evening.

77913.q: Which job from the past do these pictures mean?
77913.e: Wood, fire and black charcoal show the charcoal burner. He slowly charred wood in a kiln with little air and made charcoal this way.
77913.m: The charcoal burner made charcoal in a kiln.

77914.q: Which job from the past do these emojis mean?
77914.e: A basket of clothes by the water shows the washerwoman. Without washing machines, washerwomen washed clothes by hand in a stream or at a fountain.
77914.m: In the past, washerwomen washed the laundry by hand.

77915.q: Which craft is meant by these pictures?
77915.e: A barrel, wood and a hammer show the cooper. He makes barrels from wooden staves and iron hoops.

77916.q: Which job from the past do these emojis mean?
77916.e: Letters, horses, the post horn and mountains show the stagecoach driver. Before there was a railway, stagecoaches travelled, for example, over the Gotthard Pass.
77916.m: Stagecoach drivers blew the post horn and carried post and travellers over the passes.

77917.q: Which job do these pictures mean?
77917.e: Grain, a mill wheel and water show the miller. In the watermill, he grinds grain into flour.
77917.m: The miller grinds grain into flour.

77918.q: Which job from the past do these emojis mean?
77918.e: A horn, the night and a village show the night watchman. He walked through the lanes at night, called out the hours and sounded the alarm if there was a fire.
77918.m: The night watchman called out the hours at night.

77919.q: Which craft is meant by these pictures?
77919.e: Knotted cords and twisting show the rope maker. He twisted fibres from hemp into cords and ropes.
77919.m: The rope maker twists fibres into ropes.

77920.q: Which job do these emojis mean?
77920.e: A woman at a computer who fixes errors in the program (“bugs”) is a computer scientist. She develops and repairs software.
77920.m: Computer scientists develop programs for computers.

77921.q: Which job do these pictures mean?
77921.e: A building, a set square and a house show the architect. She plans and designs buildings.
77921.m: An architect plans and designs buildings.

77922.q: Which job do these emojis mean?
77922.e: Hair, scissors and a mirror show the hairdresser. She cuts, colours and styles hair.
77922.m: A hairdresser cuts and styles hair.

77923.q: Which job do these pictures mean?
77923.e: A gateau, a slice of cake and a cupcake show the pastry chef. She bakes and decorates gateaux and fine cakes.
77923.m: A pastry chef makes gateaux and cakes.

77924.q: Which job do these emojis mean?
77924.e: A test tube, a microscope and a lab coat show the lab technician. She carries out experiments and measurements in the laboratory.
77924.m: Lab technicians work with microscopes and test tubes.

77925.q: Which job do these pictures mean?
77925.e: Medicines, a prescription and a shop show the pharmacist. She hands out medicines and gives advice on how to take them.
77925.m: In the chemist's, pharmacists give advice about medicines.

77926.q: Which job do these emojis mean?
77926.e: Trees, a saw and a worker with a helmet show the forester. He looks after the forest and cuts down trees.
77926.m: A forester looks after the forest.

77927.q: Which job do these pictures mean?
77927.e: A newspaper, a microphone and a camera show the journalist. She researches and reports on news.
77927.m: Journalists research and report on news.

77928.q: Which sport do these pictures show?
77928.e: Volleyball and beach make beach volleyball. It is played in pairs on sand.
77928.m: In beach volleyball, two play against two on sand.

77929.q: Which team sport do these pictures show?
77929.e: Water, swimming and a ball stand for water polo. Two teams swim and throw a ball into the other team's goal.
77929.m: In water polo, you throw the ball into the goal while swimming.

77930.q: Which sport do these pictures show?
77930.e: Running in the forest with a map and compass is orienteering. You try to find checkpoints in the terrain as fast as possible.
77930.m: In orienteering, you find the checkpoints with a map and compass.

77931.q: Which sport do these pictures show?
77931.e: A sailing boat, wind and the chequered flag show sailing. The Swiss team Alinghi won the America's Cup in 2003.
77931.m: In sailing, the wind drives the boat.

77932.q: Which Swiss sport do these pictures show?
77932.e: Two fighters in sawdust from wood and a bull as a prize go with Schwingen, Swiss wrestling. The winner at the Federal Wrestling Festival often gets a bull.
77932.m: In Schwingen, two wrestlers fight in a ring of sawdust.

77933.q: Which sport do these pictures show?
77933.e: A flag in the hole and a player with a club show golf. The aim is to get the ball into the hole with as few strokes as possible.
77933.m: In golf, you need as few strokes as possible to reach the hole.

77934.q: Which competition do these pictures mean?
77934.e: A rider at a gallop and the chequered flag make a horse race. In St Moritz, horse races even take place on the frozen lake.
77934.m: In a horse race, the fastest horse wins.

77935.q: Which word do these pictures make together?
77935.e: Art (paint palette) and gymnastics make artistic gymnastics. You do exercises on apparatus such as the high bar, parallel bars and floor.
77935.m: In artistic gymnastics, you perform on different pieces of apparatus.

77936.q: Which sport do these pictures mean?
77936.e: Mountain and bike make mountain bike. You ride a mountain bike off-road and in the mountains.
77936.m: With a mountain bike you can ride over rough ground.

77937.q: Which Olympic custom do these pictures mean?
77937.e: Fire and a runner make the torch relay. The Olympic flame is lit in Olympia in Greece and carried to the host city.
77937.m: The Olympic flame is lit in Olympia.

77938.q: Which symbol do these pictures mean?
77938.e: Five rings are the symbol of the Olympic Games. They stand for the five continents that come together at the Games.
77938.m: The five Olympic rings stand for the five continents.

77939.q: Which prize for winners at the ancient Olympic Games do these pictures show?
77939.e: A Greek temple, olives and a crown show the olive wreath. In ancient Olympia, the winners received a wreath made from branches of the olive tree.
77939.m: In ancient times, Olympic winners received an olive wreath.

77940.q: Which major event do these pictures mean?
77940.e: Snow, mountains and a medal go with the Winter Olympics. In Switzerland, they took place in St Moritz in 1928 and 1948.
77940.m: St Moritz hosted the Winter Olympics twice.

77941.q: What do the best stand on at the award ceremony, as these pictures show?
77941.e: First, second and third places and a gold medal show the winners' podium. The winner stands in the middle on the highest step.
77941.m: On the winners' podium, the winner stands at the top.

77942.q: Which athletics event do these pictures show?
77942.e: A runner and several barriers stand for the hurdles. You have to jump over hurdles while running.
77942.m: In the hurdles, you jump over hurdles at full speed.

77943.q: Which athletics event do these pictures show?
77943.e: A long jump like a kangaroo's and a sandpit make long jump. After the run-up, you land in a pit of sand.
77943.m: In the long jump, you land in the sandpit.

77944.q: Which games do these pictures mean?
77944.e: A wheelchair and a medal in the stadium show the Paralympic Games. Athletes with disabilities compete there.
77944.m: At the Paralympics, people with disabilities compete.

77945.q: Which winter sport do these pictures show?
77945.e: A curling stone, a brush and ice show curling. The players sweep in front of the stone so that it slides further.
77945.m: In curling, you sweep the ice in front of the stone.

77946.q: Which winter sport do these pictures show?
77946.e: Sticks with a puck, ice and a goal show ice hockey. Each team has five outfield players and a goalkeeper on the ice.
77946.m: In ice hockey, you shoot the puck into the goal.

77947.q: Which winter sport do these pictures show?
77947.e: A sledge, the number four, ice and the chequered flag make the four-man bobsleigh. In St Moritz there is a bobsleigh run made of natural ice.
77947.m: Four people sit in a four-man bobsleigh.

77948.q: Which winter sport do these pictures mean?
77948.e: Snow and surfing make snowboarding, because you stand sideways on a board. Snowboarding has been an Olympic sport since 1998.
77948.m: In snowboarding, you stand sideways on a board.

77950.q: Which skiing event do these pictures show?
77950.e: A skier between lots of flags shows the slalom. You ski tightly around lots of gates.
77950.m: In the slalom, you ski around lots of tight gates.

77951.q: Which winter sport do these pictures mean?
77951.e: Dogs, a sledge and snow show sled dog racing. Huskies often pull the sledge.
77951.m: In sled dog racing, dogs pull the sledge.

77952.q: Which word do these pictures make together?
77952.e: Ice, speed (lightning) and running make speed skating. You skate around a 400-metre track.
77952.m: In speed skating, only the time counts.

77953.q: Which instrument do these pictures make together?
77953.e: A mouth and an organ make mouth organ, another name for the harmonica. You blow and suck air through small channels.
77953.m: You play the mouth organ with your mouth.

77954.q: Which instrument do these pictures mean?
77954.e: A church and a keyboard show the church organ. It is played with hands and feet and has lots of pipes.
77954.m: You play the organ with your hands and feet.

77955.q: Which instrument do these pictures make together?
77955.e: Bell (Glocke) and game (Spiel, the dice) make glockenspiel, a German word that is also used in English. You strike small metal bars with little mallets.
77955.m: On a glockenspiel, you strike metal bars.

77956.q: Which instrument do these pictures mean?
77956.e: The stringed instrument with a round drum and the cowboy show the banjo. It is very popular in the folk music of the USA.
77956.m: The banjo has a round body like a drum.

77957.q: Which instrument do these pictures mean?
77957.e: A stringed instrument and a very tall giraffe show the double bass. It is the largest and deepest stringed instrument in the orchestra.
77957.m: The double bass is the largest stringed instrument.

77958.q: Which instrument do these pictures mean?
77958.e: A small guitar, flowers and an island show the ukulele. It comes from Hawaii and has four strings.
77958.m: The ukulele is a small guitar from Hawaii.

77959.q: Which instrument do these pictures make together?
77959.e: Electricity (lightning) and guitar make electric guitar. It needs an amplifier so that you can hear it loudly.
77959.m: The electric guitar needs an amplifier.

77960.q: Which Swiss folk instrument do these pictures show?
77960.e: A small accordion and the mountains show the Schwyzerörgeli. It is often played in Swiss folk music.
77960.m: The Schwyzerörgeli is a small accordion from Switzerland.

77961.q: Which instrument do these pictures mean?
77961.e: A kangaroo for Australia, wood and music show the didgeridoo. It is a long wind instrument of the Aborigines made from a hollow branch.

77962.q: Which style of music do these pictures mean?
77962.e: A saxophone, a piano and a club at night go with jazz. Jazz began around 1900 in New Orleans and is all about improvising.

77963.q: Which style of music do these pictures mean?
77963.e: A microphone, a cap and a speaking head show rap. In rap, you speak words rhythmically to the music.
77963.m: In rap, you speak words to a rhythm.

77964.q: Which style of music do these pictures mean?
77964.e: A cowboy hat, a guitar and a horse go with country music. It comes from rural areas of the USA.
77964.m: Country music comes from the USA.

77965.q: Which style of music do these pictures mean?
77965.e: A violin, a piano and an old clock go with classical music. Well-known composers are Mozart and Beethoven.
77965.m: Mozart and Beethoven wrote classical music.

77966.q: Which style of music do these pictures mean?
77966.e: An island, music and the colours green, yellow and red show reggae. Reggae comes from Jamaica and became famous through Bob Marley.

77967.q: Which style of music do these pictures mean?
77967.e: Blue, a guitar and a sad face show the blues. “To have the blues” means to be sad.

77968.q: Which style of music do these pictures mean?
77968.e: A church, raised hands and music show gospel. Gospel songs are Christian songs from African American churches.
77968.m: Gospel is often sung by large choirs.

77969.q: Which style of music do these pictures mean?
77969.e: Heavy, metal and a guitar make heavy metal. Loud, distorted guitars are typical.
77969.m: Heavy metal is loud rock music with distorted guitars.

77970.q: Which famous ballet do these pictures show?
77970.e: Ballet shoes, a swan and water show “Swan Lake”. The music was written by Pyotr Tchaikovsky.
77970.m: The music for “Swan Lake” is by Tchaikovsky.

77971.q: Which Christmas ballet do these pictures show?
77971.e: A nut being cracked, ballet shoes and a Christmas tree show “The Nutcracker”. Tchaikovsky's ballet takes place on Christmas Eve.

77972.q: Which dance do these pictures mean?
77972.e: Carnival, drums, dancing and a beach go with the samba. It comes from Brazil and is danced at the carnival in Rio.

77973.q: Which dance do these pictures mean?
77973.e: Loud shoes to music show tap dance. The shoes have metal plates that click when you dance.
77973.m: In tap dance, metal plates on the shoes click.

77974.q: Which dance do these pictures mean?
77974.e: The number three, a dancing couple and violins show the waltz. It is danced in three-four time, especially in Vienna.
77974.m: The waltz is danced in three-four time.

77975.q: Which Italian folk dance do these pictures mean?
77975.e: A spider (tarantula) and dancing show the tarantella. According to an old legend, fast dancing was supposed to help against a tarantula bite.
77975.m: The tarantella is a fast dance from southern Italy.

77976.q: Which Spanish dance do these pictures mean?
77976.e: A ruffled dress, clapping, a guitar and a rose show flamenco. It comes from Andalusia in Spain.

77977.q: Which dance do these pictures mean?
77977.e: Acrobatics, spins, a cap and music show breakdance. It is part of hip-hop culture from New York.
77977.m: Breakdance is part of hip-hop culture.

77979.q: Which dice game do these pictures show?
77979.e: Snakes, ladders and a dice show snakes and ladders. You climb up the ladders and slide down the snakes.
77979.m: In snakes and ladders, you slide down the snakes.

77980.q: Which board game do these pictures mean?
77980.e: A pawn, a king and a horse show chess. The horse is called the knight, and you want to checkmate the king.
77980.m: In chess, you want to checkmate the king.

77983.q: Which Swiss card game do these pictures mean?
77983.e: Playing cards with roses, acorns, bells and shields show Jass. It is the best-known card game in Switzerland.
77983.m: Jass is the most popular card game in Switzerland.

77984.q: Which puzzle game do these pictures mean?
77984.e: A puzzle piece and a picture show the jigsaw puzzle. You put lots of small pieces together to make a whole picture.
77984.m: In a jigsaw puzzle, you put pieces together to make a picture.

77986.q: Which device do these pictures make together?
77986.e: Needle, thread and a machine make sewing machine. With it, you sew fabric much faster than by hand.
77986.m: With a sewing machine you sew faster than by hand.

77987.q: Which hobby do these pictures show?
77987.e: A fishing rod, a fish and a river show fishing. In Switzerland you usually need a licence for it.
77987.m: In Switzerland you usually need a licence to go fishing.

77988.q: Which hobby do these pictures show?
77988.e: A seedling, a potted plant and water show gardening. Plants need soil, light and water.
77988.m: In gardening, you look after plants.

77989.q: What are you building, as these pictures show?
77989.e: A bird, a house and a hammer make the birdhouse. In winter you can feed birds in it.
77989.m: You build a birdhouse for birds.

77990.q: Which hobby do these pictures show?
77990.e: Scissors, paper and coloured pencils show crafts. You cut, stick and paint.
77990.m: In crafts, you cut and stick.

77991.q: Which word do these pictures make together?
77991.e: Climbing and wall make climbing wall. In climbing centres there are walls with colourful holds.
77991.m: On a climbing wall, you hold on to holds.

77992.q: Which leisure activity do these pictures show?
77992.e: A kite and wind show kite flying. In autumn it is often windy enough for it.
77992.m: You need wind to fly a kite.

77994.q: Which paper craft do these pictures mean?
77994.e: Paper, a bird and Japan show origami. In this Japanese art, you fold figures such as the crane out of paper.
77994.m: Origami is the Japanese art of paper folding.

77995.q: Which word do these pictures make together?
77995.e: Air (aeroplane) and port (anchor) make airport. The largest airport in Switzerland is in Zurich.
77995.m: The largest airport in Switzerland is near Zurich.

77996.q: Which word do these pictures make together?
77996.e: Train and ticket make train ticket. In Switzerland, people say “Billett” for a ticket.
77996.m: You need a ticket to travel by train.

77997.q: Which travel document do these pictures mean?
77997.e: Passport control, a red booklet and a suitcase show the passport. The Swiss passport is red.

77998.q: Which book do these pictures mean?
77998.e: Travel, a book and good tips make a travel guide. It describes the sights at a holiday destination.
77998.m: A travel guide gives tips for your destination.

77999.q: Which famous Swiss train do these pictures mean?
77999.e: A glacier, a train and mountains show the Glacier Express. It runs from Zermatt to St Moritz and is said to be the slowest express train in the world.
77999.m: The Glacier Express runs from Zermatt to St Moritz.

78000.q: What kind of journey do these pictures show?
78000.e: A big ship, the sea and islands show a cruise. You travel on a ship and visit several places.
78000.m: On a cruise, you live on a ship.

78001.q: Which travel problem do these pictures mean?
78001.e: Flying, a different time and tiredness show jet lag. It happens when you fly quickly across several time zones.
78001.m: Jet lag comes from flights across time zones.

78002.q: Which means of transport do these pictures make together?
78002.e: Cable, car and mountain make cable car. The cabin hangs from cables and travels up the mountain.
78002.m: On a cable car, the cabin hangs from cables.

78003.q: Which holiday activity do these pictures show?
78003.e: Hiking boots, a mountain and a map show hiking. Switzerland has a dense network of footpaths marked in yellow.
78003.m: Swiss footpaths are marked in yellow.

78004.q: Which word do these pictures make together?
78004.e: Air and bed (mattress) make airbed. You can lie on it by the water or sleep on it in a tent.
78004.m: An airbed is filled with air.

78005.q: Which word do these pictures make together?
78005.e: Sun and umbrella make sun umbrella. It gives shade on the beach or in the garden.

78006.q: What kind of holiday do these pictures show?
78006.e: A tent, a campfire and a forest show a camp. The Scouts, for example, often go to camp in summer.
78006.m: At camp, you sleep in a tent.

78008.q: Which feeling on holiday do these pictures mean?
78008.e: A house, a thought and sadness show homesickness. You miss your home, for example at camp.
78008.m: Homesickness means you miss your home.

78009.e: A postbox, a picture and the beach show the picture postcard. It shows a picture of the holiday place and is sent by post.
78009.m: People like to send a postcard from their holidays.

78010.q: Which holiday problem do these pictures mean?
78010.e: Lots of cars and a snail show the traffic jam. At the start of the holidays, there are often traffic jams in front of the Gotthard road tunnel.
78010.m: At the start of the holidays, there are often traffic jams at the Gotthard.

78011.q: Which festival do these pictures mean?
78011.e: A pumpkin, sweets and a ghost show Halloween. It is celebrated on 31 October.

78012.q: Which festival do these pictures mean?
78012.e: Masks, drums, trumpets and confetti show carnival (Fasnacht). The Basel carnival has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage since 2017.

78013.q: Which public holiday do these pictures mean?
78013.e: The numbers 1 and 8, fireworks and paper lanterns show Swiss National Day on 1 August. It is the national holiday of Switzerland.
78013.m: Switzerland's national holiday is on 1 August.

78014.q: Which Zurich festival do these pictures mean?
78014.e: A snowman in the fire, horses and six o'clock show Sechseläuten. At 6 p.m., the Böögg is set alight, and riders circle the fire.
78014.m: At Sechseläuten, the Böögg is burnt.

78015.q: Which market in Bern do these pictures mean?
78015.e: Onions, shopping and the bear for Bern show the Zibelemärit, the onion market. It takes place every year on the fourth Monday in November.
78015.m: The Zibelemärit is an onion market in Bern.

78016.q: Which Swiss custom do these pictures mean?
78016.e: Decorated cows with bells coming down the mountain show the Alpine descent. In autumn, the animals come back from the Alpine pastures to the valley.
78016.m: In the Alpine descent, the cows return to the valley in autumn.

78017.q: Who comes on 6 December with these pictures?
78017.e: A man with a beard, mandarins and nuts show the Samichlaus, the Swiss St Nicholas. He comes on 6 December, often together with Schmutzli.

78018.q: Which festival do these pictures mean?
78018.e: A big wheel, a merry-go-round and sweets show the Chilbi. That is what a funfair is called in Switzerland.
78018.m: A Chilbi is a funfair with rides.

78019.q: Which time of the church year do these pictures mean?
78019.e: Fir branches, candles and the number four show Advent. The Advent wreath has four candles for the four Sundays before Christmas.
78019.m: Four candles burn on the Advent wreath.

78021.q: Which word do these pictures make together?
78021.e: Hearing (ear) and book make audiobook. A book is read aloud and you listen.
78021.m: You listen to an audiobook instead of reading it.

78022.q: Which place do these pictures mean?
78022.e: A clapperboard, popcorn and a ticket show the cinema. There you watch films on a big screen.
78022.m: At the cinema, you watch films on a screen.

78023.q: What kind of photo do these pictures mean?
78023.e: If you point your mobile at yourself, you take a selfie. A selfie is a photo you take of yourself.
78023.m: A selfie is a photo of yourself.

78024.q: Which word do these pictures make together?
78024.e: Computer and game (controller) make computer game. With games, you should pay attention to the recommended age.
78024.m: With computer games, you check the age rating.

78025.q: What kind of film do these pictures mean?
78025.e: A pencil, a film strip and a mouse show the cartoon. Lots of drawn pictures are shown quickly one after another.
78025.m: A cartoon is made of lots of drawn pictures.

78026.q: What kind of film do these pictures mean?
78026.e: No sound, a film strip and a hat like Charlie Chaplin's show the silent film. Until the end of the 1920s, films mostly had no spoken sound.
78026.m: Silent films have no spoken sound.

78027.q: Which programme do these pictures mean?
78027.e: Sun and clouds, a television and a map show the weather forecast. It predicts the weather for the next few days.
78027.m: The weather forecast predicts the weather.

78028.q: Which German saying with animals, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture puzzle?
78028.e: A dog and a hole in the ground stand for the German saying “There lies the dog buried”. It means you have found the real heart or cause of a problem.
78028.m: If you know where the dog is buried, you know the real cause of a problem.

78029.q: Which German saying with animals, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture puzzle?
a: Have a frog in your throat
78029.e: A frog, a microphone and a face without a mouth show that someone can hardly speak. As in English, “having a frog in your throat” means being hoarse or briefly losing your voice.
78029.m: If you have a frog in your throat, you are hoarse and need to clear your throat.

78030.q: Which German saying with animals, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture puzzle?
a: Have a chicken to pluck with someone
Go to bed with the hens
The hen that lays golden eggs
78030.e: A hen, a feather and an angry face stand for “plucking a chicken”. If you have a chicken to pluck with someone, you still have a quarrel to settle with them, like “having a bone to pick” in English.
78030.m: If you have a chicken to pluck with someone, you still need to sort out something unpleasant with them.

78031.q: Which German saying with animals, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture puzzle?
a: Ten horses couldn't drag me there
Don't look a gift horse in the mouth
78031.e: A horse and arrows for “from behind” and “the wrong way round” stand for “bridling the horse from behind”. It means doing things in the wrong order, like “putting the cart before the horse”.
78031.m: If you bridle the horse from behind, you start a task at the wrong end.

78032.q: Which German saying with animals, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture puzzle?
a: Be as strong as a bear
78032.e: A bear, a rucksack to tie on and a lying face with a long nose stand for “tying a bear on someone”. It means telling someone a made-up story as if it were true.
78032.m: If you tie a bear on someone, you are telling them a lie.

78033.q: Which German saying with animals, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture puzzle?
a: Where fox and hare say good night
78033.e: A fox, a hare and the moon show the two animals saying good night to each other. The saying describes a very remote, lonely place.
78033.m: Where fox and hare say good night, hardly any people live.

78034.q: Which German saying with animals, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture puzzle?
a: Stand there like a drenched poodle
78034.e: A poodle, water and a sad face make the “drenched poodle”. Someone who stands there like that is ashamed, disappointed and subdued.
78034.m: Someone who stands there like a drenched poodle looks ashamed and downcast.

78035.q: Which German saying with animals, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture puzzle?
78035.e: The oyster stands for pearls, the pigs for the swine. “Casting pearls before swine” means giving something valuable to someone who does not appreciate it; the saying comes from the Sermon on the Mount and exists in English too.
78035.m: If you cast pearls before swine, you waste something valuable on people who do not appreciate it.

78036.q: Which German saying with animals, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture puzzle?
78036.e: A sleeping dog and an alarm clock make “waking sleeping dogs”. It means drawing attention to something for no reason and so causing trouble, like the English “let sleeping dogs lie”.
78036.m: If you wake sleeping dogs, you draw other people's attention to something unnecessarily.

78038.q: Which German saying with body parts, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
a: Tear out a leg for something
Stand on both legs in life
Take your legs in your hands
78038.e: A leg, a tense muscle and a sweating face show great effort. “Tearing out a leg” means trying extremely hard, like “bending over backwards”.
78038.m: If you tear out a leg for something, you make an extraordinary effort.

78039.q: Which German saying with body parts, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
78039.e: A person, a nose and a dancer make “dancing around on someone's nose”. It means treating someone without respect and doing whatever you like.
78039.m: If you dance around on other people's noses, you show them no consideration.

78040.q: Which German saying with body parts, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
a: Bury your head in the sand
78040.e: Soap, a person, a loud voice and an angry face make “washing someone's head”. It means telling someone off sharply.
78040.m: If you wash someone's head, you give them a piece of your mind.

78041.q: Which German saying with body parts, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
78041.e: The face with bared teeth and the muscle show grim determination and strength. “Biting your teeth together” means bravely putting up with pain or hardship, like “gritting your teeth”.
78041.m: If you bite your teeth together, you keep going despite difficulties.

78042.q: Which German saying with body parts, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
a: Have a board in front of your head
Want to go through the wall with your head
78042.e: A person, a piece of wood and a puzzled face make the “board in front of your head”. Someone who has one fails to understand something obvious.
78042.m: If you have a board in front of your head, you don't understand something very simple.

78043.q: Which German saying with body parts, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
78043.e: Helping hands, an arm and an upward arrow show how you support someone. “Grabbing someone under the arms” means helping them in a difficult situation.
78043.m: If you grab someone under the arms, you help them out of a tight spot.

78044.q: Which German saying with body parts, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
a: Suck something out of your fingers
78044.e: A finger at the mouth and a thought bubble show something being sucked out of a finger and thought up. The saying means inventing something freely, like “pulling something out of thin air”.
78044.m: If you suck something out of your fingers, you make it up without any basis.

78045.q: Which German saying about food, translated word for word, do these emojis encode?
a: That's all the same to me
78045.e: A talking person, cheese and rolling eyes make “That's just cheese”. Germans use it to call a statement nonsense.
78045.m: If something is cheese, you think it is nonsense.

78046.q: Which German saying about food, translated word for word, do these emojis encode?
a: A land flowing with milk and honey
78046.e: Honey, a mouth and a person show honey being spread around someone's mouth. It means flattering someone to get something, like “buttering someone up”.
78046.m: If you smear honey around other people's mouths, you flatter them on purpose.

78047.q: Which German saying about food, translated word for word, do these emojis encode?
a: Be the yellow of the egg
78047.e: A salad and a desperate face make “Now we have the salad”. People say it when a feared muddle or mishap has happened.
78047.m: If you have the salad, a mess has happened.

78048.q: Which German saying about food, translated word for word, do these emojis encode?
a: Throw the sausage at the side of bacon
78048.e: A sausage, scales and a trophy stand for a decision about who wins. “It's about the sausage” means the decisive moment has come; probably because a sausage used to be a common prize at fairs and contests.
78048.m: When it's about the sausage, the decision is happening now.

78049.q: Which German saying about food, translated word for word, do these emojis encode?
a: Find a hair in the soup
Be born with a golden spoon in your mouth
78049.e: A soup, a spoon and a pained face show that you have to eat something unpleasant. “Spooning out the soup you crumbled in yourself” means facing the consequences of your own actions, like “you've made your bed, now lie in it”.
78049.m: If you have to spoon out the soup, you bear the consequences of your own mistake.

78050.q: Which German saying about food, translated word for word, do these emojis encode?
a: Cut yourself a piece of the cake
78050.e: A pastry, grapes for raisins and two picking fingers make “picking out the raisins”. It means choosing only the best and leaving the rest to others, like “cherry-picking”.
78050.m: If you pick out the raisins, you take only the best for yourself.

78051.q: Which German saying about food, translated word for word, do these emojis encode?
a: Feel like a fish in water
78051.e: Butter, fish and a talking person make the northern German saying “Butter with the fish”. It is a call to finally speak plainly and get to the point.
78051.m: Someone who says “Butter with the fish” wants you to get to the point at last.

78052.q: Which German saying about food, translated word for word, do these emojis encode?
a: Others only cook with water too
Cook something on a small flame
78052.e: Water, a cooking pot and a cook make “Others only cook with water too”. It means that even people who seem superior have no better means than you.
78052.m: Others only cook with water too, so you don't need to hide from them.

78053.q: Which German saying about nature, translated word for word, is in these pictures?
a: Not see the forest for all the trees
You don't transplant an old tree
78053.e: Lots of trees and a little monkey covering its eyes show someone who sees nothing because of all the trees. As in English (“can't see the wood for the trees”), it means missing the main point because of lots of details.
78053.m: If you can't see the forest for the trees, you miss what is obvious.

78054.q: Which German saying about nature, translated word for word, is in these pictures?
78054.e: A mountain, a hiker and a tick show that the mountain has been crossed. In German, “being over the mountain” means the worst is over.
78054.m: If you are over the mountain, the hardest part is behind you.

78055.q: Which German saying about nature, translated word for word, is in these pictures?
78055.e: A rose, a speech bubble and a quiet face show something being said carefully via a flower. “Saying something through the flower” means hinting at criticism only indirectly.
78055.m: If you say something through the flower, you say it politely and indirectly.

78056.q: Which German saying about nature, translated word for word, is in these pictures?
a: Shoot out of the ground like mushrooms
Lose the ground under your feet
Stamp something out of the ground
78056.e: Several mushrooms and an upward arrow show lots of mushrooms coming up at once. It describes things that suddenly appear in large numbers, like “springing up like mushrooms”.
78056.m: Things that shoot out of the ground like mushrooms suddenly turn up everywhere.

78057.q: Which German saying about nature, translated word for word, is in these pictures?
a: Have built close to the water
The water is up to your neck
78057.e: A quiet face, water and an arrow pointing down make “Still waters are deep”. The proverb, also known in English as “still waters run deep”, says that reserved people often have more thoughts or skills than you would expect.
78057.m: Still waters are deep, because quiet people can surprise you.

78058.q: Which German saying about nature, translated word for word, is in these pictures?
78058.e: Lots of drops, a stone and a hole show how water slowly hollows out the stone. The proverb says that perseverance achieves great things; it goes back to the Latin “Gutta cavat lapidem”.
78058.m: Constant dripping hollows the stone, so persistence pays off.

78059.q: Which German saying about nature, translated word for word, is in these pictures?
a: Take the path of least resistance
A stone falls from my heart
78059.e: A stone on a path in front of a walking person shows an obstacle. “Laying stones in someone's path” means deliberately making things difficult for them.
78059.m: If you lay stones in other people's paths, you make their plans harder.

78060.q: Which German saying about nature, translated word for word, is in these pictures?
a: Be able to pull out trees
The apple doesn't fall far from the trunk
You don't transplant an old tree
Trees aren't allowed to grow into the sky
78060.e: A tree, a strong arm and a happy face show someone full of energy. Someone who “could pull out trees” feels very strong and eager to act.
78060.m: If you could pull out trees, you are full of strength and energy.

78061.q: Which German saying about money, translated word for word, is encoded here?
a: Put something on the high edge
Bash your money on the head
78061.e: A money bag, a cupboard and an upward arrow show money being stored high up. “Putting something on the high edge” means saving money.
78061.m: If you put money on the high edge, you save it for later.

78062.q: Which Swiss saying about money, translated word for word, is encoded here?
78062.e: A coin and two turning arrows show each coin being turned over twice. The Rappen is the Swiss cent; someone who turns every Rappen over twice is very thrifty.
78062.m: If you turn every Rappen over twice, you don't like spending money.

78065.q: Which German saying about money, translated word for word, is encoded here?
a: Hang something on the big bell
78065.e: A piece of chalk, a bill and a worried face make “standing in the chalk”. Innkeepers used to write their guests' debts on a board in chalk; the saying means being in debt.
78065.m: If you stand in the chalk with someone, you owe them money.

78066.q: Which German saying about money, translated word for word, is encoded here?
a: Pay back in the same coin
The other side of the medal
78066.e: A coin, a tick for “valid” and a thoughtful face make “taking something for cash coin”. It means believing something is true or meant seriously without checking, like “taking it at face value”.
78066.m: If you take everything for cash coin, you believe every statement literally.

78067.q: Which German saying about money, translated word for word, is encoded here?
a: Tear a hole in your purse
78067.e: A purse and a hole make “tearing a hole in your purse”. People say it when something costs a great deal of money.
78067.m: An expensive purchase tears a hole in your purse.

78068.q: Which German saying about money, translated word for word, is encoded here?
a: Money alone doesn't make you happy
78068.e: A money bag, a crown for ruling and the Earth make “Money rules the world”. The proverb means that money has great influence everywhere, like “money makes the world go round”.
78068.m: The proverb “Money rules the world” complains about the power of money.

78069.q: Which German saying about work, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
78069.e: A sloth on a sofa makes “lying on the lazy skin”. It means being idle and not working.
78069.m: If you lie on the lazy skin, you do nothing.

78070.q: Which German saying about work, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
78070.e: A sprig for the laurel wreath, a trophy and a sleeping face make “resting on your laurels”. As in English, it means slacking off after a success and doing nothing more.
78070.m: If you rest on your laurels, you relax for too long after a success.

78071.q: Which German saying about work, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
a: Shake something out of your sleeve
78071.e: A shirt, an arm and an upward arrow show sleeves pushed up. As in English, “rolling up your sleeves” means getting down to work energetically.
78071.m: If you roll up your sleeves, you tackle a task with determination.

78072.q: Which German saying about work, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
78072.e: A hammer, a pin with a head and a tick make “making nails with heads”. It means finishing something thoroughly and properly.
78072.m: If you make nails with heads, you do a job properly and completely.

78073.q: Which German saying about work, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
78073.e: The bowling ball and a sleeping face make “pushing a quiet ball”. It means not making much effort at work.
78073.m: If you push a quiet ball, you work at a leisurely pace without stress.

78074.q: Which German saying about work, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
78074.e: A ball, a runner and a repeat sign show someone who keeps following the ball. In German, “staying on the ball” means sticking with something persistently.
78074.m: If you stay on the ball, you keep pursuing your goal with stamina.

78075.q: Which German saying about work, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
a: Rattling is part of the craft
78075.e: A tool for the craft and shouting and a loudspeaker for loud rattling make the proverb. It means you also have to advertise your work.
78075.m: Rattling is part of the craft, so you have to draw attention to what you do.

78076.q: Which German saying about work, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
78076.e: Eyes, a finger and a person in an office show someone being watched closely at work. “Looking at someone's fingers” means checking on them strictly.
78076.m: If you look at someone's fingers, you check their work closely.

78077.q: Which German saying about time, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
a: Push something onto the long bench
78077.e: A seat, an arrow for pushing and an hourglass make “pushing something onto the long bench”. It means putting off a task again and again.
78077.m: If you push something onto the long bench, you don't do it in time.

78078.q: Which German saying about time, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
78078.e: A clock at twelve, the number five and a warning sign make “It's five to twelve”. Germans say this when it is high time to act, like “at the eleventh hour”.
78078.m: When it's five to twelve, you must act at once.

78079.q: Which German saying about time, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
a: All good things come in threes
78079.e: The infinity sign, a plus, the three and a calendar make “forever and three days”. The saying is an exaggerated way to describe a very long time.
78079.m: If you wait forever and three days, you wait a very long time.

78080.q: Which German saying about time, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
a: A good thing wants a while
He who laughs last laughs best
78080.e: A nice thing, an hourglass and a slow tortoise make “A good thing wants a while”. The proverb says that good work takes time.
78080.m: A good thing wants a while, so you shouldn't rush good things.

78081.q: Which German saying about time, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
a: Tomorrow, tomorrow, just not today, say all the lazy people
Everything was better in the old days
78081.e: The morning, an arrow to a later day on the calendar and a sleeping face show someone who puts everything off. The saying criticises laziness and putting things off.
78081.m: Someone who always says “tomorrow” comfortably puts off their duties.

78082.q: Which German saying about time, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
a: Slam the door in someone's face
Sweep in front of your own door
78082.e: A door, a hurrying person, a stopwatch and a speech bubble show a short chat in passing. “Between door and hinge” means in a hurry and on the side.
78082.m: Something discussed between door and hinge gets little time.

78083.q: Which German saying about time, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
a: Don't praise the day before the evening
In the evening the lazy get busy
78083.e: Sun, applause, moon and a cross show: don't praise the day before evening has come. The proverb warns against celebrating a success too early, like “don't count your chickens before they hatch”.
78083.m: Don't praise the day before the evening, because a lot can still change.

78084.q: Which German saying about time, translated word for word, is hidden in this picture?
a: At the last press of the button
78084.e: An alarm clock, a pressing finger and the chequered flag show that someone only acts just before the end. The saying means at the very last moment.
78084.m: If you do everything at the last press of the button, you easily get stressed.

78085.q: Which German weather saying, translated word for word, do these emojis hide?
a: A storm in a water glass
People in glass houses shouldn't throw stones
78085.e: A whirlwind and a glass make the “storm in a water glass”. It means a lot of fuss about something unimportant, like the English “storm in a teacup”.
78085.m: A storm in a water glass is a lot of fuss about very little.

78086.q: Which German weather saying, translated word for word, do these emojis hide?
a: The sun brings it to light
78086.e: Rain, an arrow and then sun make “After rain comes sunshine”. The proverb comforts people that better times follow hard ones.
78086.m: After rain comes sunshine, so you should keep hoping in hard times.

78087.q: Which German weather saying, translated word for word, do these emojis hide?
a: Whoever sows wind will reap storm
Make a lot of wind about nothing
78087.e: Wind, seeds and an arrow to a whirlwind make “Whoever sows wind will reap storm”. The saying from the Bible (Book of Hosea), in English “sow the wind and reap the whirlwind”, warns that bad deeds have even worse consequences.
78087.m: Whoever sows wind will reap storm, because bad deeds come back even stronger.

78088.q: Which German weather saying, translated word for word, do these emojis hide?
78088.e: A thunderstorm, a loud voice and an angry face make a “thunderstorm”. Someone who lets loose a thunderstorm tells people off fiercely.
78088.m: Someone who lets loose a thunderstorm scolds loudly and fiercely.

78089.q: Which German weather saying, translated word for word, do these emojis hide?
a: Hold all the threads in your hand
78089.e: Rain and a thread make “It's raining strings”. It describes heavy, dense rain that falls from the sky like cords, like “raining cats and dogs”.
78089.m: When it's raining strings, it is pouring down.

78090.q: Which German weather saying, translated word for word, do these emojis hide?
a: Know where the wind blows from
78090.e: Wind, a question mark and a compass show the question of where the wind comes from. “Knowing where the wind blows from” means seeing through the real situation or other people's intentions.
78090.m: If you know where the wind blows from, you know the real situation.

78091.q: Which German weather saying, translated word for word, do these emojis hide?
a: Fall out of all the clouds
Have your head in the clouds
Grab something out of the air
78091.e: A cloud, a downward arrow and an astonished face make “falling out of all the clouds”. It means being completely surprised or disappointed.
78091.m: If you fall out of all the clouds, you are completely surprised.

78092.q: Which German weather saying, translated word for word, do these emojis hide?
a: A silver streak on the horizon
The morning hour has gold in its mouth
78092.e: A bright streak on the horizon, sparkles and a confident face make the “silver streak on the horizon”. It stands for a first sign of hope, a bit like a silver lining.
78092.m: A silver streak on the horizon gives you hope again.

78093.q: Which German saying with a colour, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
a: Get green and blue with anger
Promise the blue from the sky
78093.e: The colour blue, a bed and a calendar show a day spent in bed. “Making blue” means staying away from work or school without an excuse.
78093.m: Someone who makes blue stays away from work without a good reason.

78094.q: Which German saying with a colour, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
a: Not the yellow of the egg
78094.e: An egg, the colour yellow and a thumbs down make “not the yellow of the egg”. Something like that is not the best solution.
78094.m: Something that is not the yellow of the egg is not quite convincing.

78095.q: Which German saying with a colour, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
a: Not get onto a green branch
78095.e: The colour green, a branch and a cross make “not getting onto a green branch”. It means having no success despite trying hard.
78095.m: If you never get onto a green branch, you simply have no success.

78096.q: Which German saying with a colour, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
a: Be up to both ears in work
78096.e: The colour green, an ear and a baby make “being green behind the ears”. Someone like that is still young and inexperienced, “wet behind the ears” in English.
78096.m: If you are green behind the ears, you have little experience.

78097.q: Which German saying with a colour, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
a: Take the bull by the horns
78097.e: A red cloth and a bull recall bullfighting. If something is “a red cloth” to someone, it provokes and annoys them a lot, like “a red rag to a bull”.
78097.m: Something that is a red cloth to someone makes them furious at once.

78098.q: Which saying with a colour does this picture puzzle show?
78098.e: Among several sheep, a black one stands out. “The black sheep” is someone who stands out in a group in a bad way.
78098.m: The black sheep of a family stands out because of bad behaviour.

78099.q: Which German saying with a colour, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
78099.e: The colour blue, a shocked face and sparkles for a miracle make “experiencing your blue miracle”. It means getting a nasty surprise.
78099.m: If you experience your blue miracle, you get an unpleasant surprise.

78100.q: Which German saying with a colour, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
a: Chase someone into the goat's horn
78100.e: A bus, the colour blue and a question mark show a journey with an unknown destination. A “trip into the blue” is an outing where you don't know the destination beforehand.
78100.m: On a trip into the blue, you don't know where you are going.

78101.q: Which German saying with a colour, translated word for word, does this picture puzzle show?
78101.e: The colour red, numbers and a falling curve make “writing red numbers”. Losses used to be entered in red in the accounts, so the saying means making a loss, like “being in the red”.
78101.m: A company that writes red numbers is making a loss.

78102.q: Which Latin proverb is shown in pictures here?
78102.e: A runner and a snail combine haste and slowness. “Festina lente” means “make haste slowly”; according to Suetonius it was one of Emperor Augustus's favourite sayings.
78102.m: Festina lente advises acting quickly but with care.

78103.q: Which Latin proverb is shown in pictures here?
78103.e: Coming, seeing and conquering are shown by walking, eyes and a trophy. Julius Caesar is said to have written “Veni, vidi, vici” (I came, I saw, I conquered) in 47 BC after a quick victory.
78103.m: With “Veni, vidi, vici” Caesar reported a lightning victory.

78104.q: Which Latin proverb is shown in pictures here?
78104.e: Money, a nose and a cross make “Money doesn't stink”, in Latin “Pecunia non olet”. The saying is attributed to Emperor Vespasian, who taxed public toilets.
78104.m: Pecunia non olet means that you can't tell where money comes from.

78105.q: Which Latin proverb is shown in pictures here?
78105.e: A brain for the mind and running and muscles for the body make “Mens sana in corpore sano”. The phrase comes from Juvenal's Satires and means “a healthy mind in a healthy body”.
78105.m: Mens sana in corpore sano links mental and physical health.

78106.q: Which Latin proverb is shown in pictures here?
78106.e: A falling dice and a river recall Caesar at the Rubicon in 49 BC. “Alea iacta est” means “The die is cast” and says that a decision has been made that cannot be undone.
78106.m: People say alea iacta est when there is no going back.

78107.q: Which Latin proverb is shown in pictures here?
78107.e: A person, a hand on the head and a cross for the mistake show that mistakes are part of being human. “Errare humanum est” means “To err is human”; similar thoughts can already be found in Cicero and Seneca.
78107.m: Errare humanum est reminds us that everyone makes mistakes.

78108.q: Which Latin proverb is shown in pictures here?
78108.e: Rocks, a climber and a star show the hard way up. “Per aspera ad astra” means “Through hardships to the stars”, in other words through effort to success.
78108.m: Per aspera ad astra means that the road to success is often hard.

78109.q: Which Latin proverb is shown in pictures here?
a: Quod licet Iovi, non licet bovi
78109.e: A name tag and a crystal ball make name and omen. “Nomen est omen” means “The name is a sign” and goes back to the poet Plautus.
78109.m: People say nomen est omen when a name suits the person who has it.

78110.q: Which English idiom do these pictures show?
a: Let the cat out of the bag
It never rains but it pours
78110.e: Rain, a cat and a dog make “It's raining cats and dogs”. The idiom means it is pouring with rain.
78110.m: When it's raining cats and dogs, it is bucketing down.

78111.q: Which English idiom do these pictures show?
a: To have your cake and eat it
78111.e: A slice of cake and the sign for “really easy” make “a piece of cake”. The idiom means something is very easy.
78111.m: Something that is a piece of cake works without any effort.

78112.q: Which English idiom do these pictures show?
78112.e: A leg, a bang for breaking and the theatre masks make “Break a leg”. People use this idiom, especially in the theatre, to wish someone good luck before a performance.
78112.m: With “Break a leg” you wish actors good luck.

78113.q: Which English idiom do these pictures show?
78113.e: The colour blue and the full moon make the “blue moon”. That is the name for a rare second full moon in a month, so “once in a blue moon” means very rarely.
78113.m: Something that happens once in a blue moon happens only very rarely.

78114.q: Which English idiom do these pictures show?
78114.e: An elephant in the living room and a closed mouth make “the elephant in the room”. It means an obvious problem that nobody wants to talk about.
78114.m: The elephant in the room is a big problem that everyone keeps quiet about.

78115.q: Which English idiom do these pictures show?
78115.e: A fist for “hit” and books make “hit the books”. The idiom means to study hard.
78115.m: If you hit the books before an exam, you study hard.

78116.q: Which English idiom do these pictures show?
78116.e: A weather symbol and a sick face make “under the weather”. The idiom means feeling unwell or slightly ill.
78116.m: If you are under the weather, you don't feel quite well.

78117.q: Which English idiom do these pictures show?
a: To cost an arm and a leg
78117.e: An arm, a leg and a money bag make “to cost an arm and a leg”. The idiom means that something is extremely expensive.
78117.m: Something that costs an arm and a leg is very expensive.

78118.q: Which English idiom do these pictures show?
78118.e: A pig and an aeroplane show a flying pig. “When pigs fly” means “never”, because pigs cannot fly.
78118.m: When pigs fly means that something will certainly never happen.

78119.q: Which Swiss German saying, translated word for word, is encoded in this picture?
a: If it doesn't help, it doesn't hurt
78119.e: A goat, a licking tongue and a cross show: no goat can lick that away. The saying means that a fact is fixed and cannot be changed.
78119.m: Something no goat can lick away is an undeniable fact.

78120.q: Which Swiss German saying, translated word for word, is encoded in this picture?
a: The faster one is the quicker one
78120.e: Two identical men, a double arrow and a shrug show that the two can be swapped. “That's Hans as Heiri” means it makes no difference.
78120.m: If something is Hans as Heiri, it doesn't matter which you choose.

78121.q: Which Swiss German saying, translated word for word, is encoded in this picture?
a: If it doesn't help, it doesn't hurt
Among the rich you learn to save
78121.e: A laughing face, an arrow and a stop sign show that the fun is over. With “Now the fun is finished” people make it clear that things are serious now.
78121.m: Someone who says “Now the fun is finished” is putting an end to the fun.

78122.q: Which Swiss German saying, translated word for word, is encoded in this picture?
a: The faster one is the quicker one
There's some as long as there's some
78122.e: A tortoise, a warding-off gesture and a runner show: just don't rush. “Nume nid gsprängt” is a well-known saying from Bern and means “Just don't hurry”.
78122.m: Just don't rush advises going about things calmly and without haste.

78123.q: Which Swiss German saying, translated word for word, is encoded in this picture?
a: You can hang on my rucksack
78123.e: Two foxes and a waste basket show that something is worthless and can be thrown away. “That's for the foxes” means that the effort was wasted.
78123.m: Something that is for the foxes was wasted effort.

78124.q: Which Swiss German saying, translated word for word, is encoded in this picture?
a: That doesn't make the roast fat
If it doesn't help, it doesn't hurt
78124.e: A roast, a tiny amount and a shrug show that such a small amount won't make the roast fat. The saying means that something hardly matters.
78124.m: Something that doesn't make the roast fat makes hardly any difference.

78125.q: Which Swiss German saying, translated word for word, is encoded in this picture?
a: A lot of water will flow down the Limmat before then
Among the rich you learn to save
78125.e: Flowing water, an hourglass and the city of Zurich on the river Limmat show a long period of time. The saying means that it will be a long time before something happens.
78125.m: A lot of water will flow down the Limmat before then, so there is plenty of time.

78126.q: Which Swiss German saying, translated word for word, is encoded in this picture?
a: The faster one is the quicker one
If everyone looks after themselves, everyone is looked after
78126.e: A runner, a gold medal and a stopwatch show that the fastest wins. “The faster one is the quicker one” means: whoever comes first gets something, like “first come, first served”.
78126.m: The faster one is the quicker one, so it pays to be early.

78127.q: Which Swiss German saying, translated word for word, is encoded in this picture?
a: There's some as long as there's some
You can hang on my rucksack
78127.e: Biscuits, a box and an hourglass running out show a supply that is coming to an end. The saying means that there is only something as long as stocks last.
78127.m: There's some as long as there's some, so help yourself in good time.

78128.q: Which novel of world literature do these emojis show?
78128.e: A bearded knight on a horse fights against something that turns in the wind: Don Quixote thinks windmills are giants and attacks them.
78128.m: Miguel de Cervantes published the first part of “Don Quixote” in 1605.

78129.q: Which novel do these emojis show?
78129.e: A white whale, a ship, a leg and a bearded captain: Captain Ahab hunts the white whale that cost him his leg.

78130.q: Which Latin American novel do these pictures mean?
a: Love in the Time of Cholera
78130.e: A hundred years in the invented village of Macondo: over generations the Buendía family experiences strange things, such as swarms of yellow butterflies.
78130.m: Gabriel García Márquez published the novel about the Buendía family in 1967.

78131.q: Which novel do these emojis show?
78131.e: Quasimodo rings the cathedral bells, and the dancer Esmeralda is accompanied by her goat Djali.
78131.m: The novel's original title is “Notre-Dame de Paris”, and it came out in 1831.

78132.q: Which adventure novel fits these pictures?
a: The Man in the Iron Mask
78132.e: Edmond Dantès is imprisoned in a fortress although innocent, escapes, finds a treasure on an island and returns as a noble count.
78132.m: Alexandre Dumas published “The Count of Monte Cristo” from 1844 to 1846.

78133.q: Which work of world literature do these emojis show?

a: A Song of Ice and Fire

78139.m: J. R. R. Tolkien published “The Lord of the Rings” in three volumes in 1954 and 1955.

78144.e: A young man stays young and handsome while his painted portrait ages in his place.
78144.m: Oscar Wilde's only novel first appeared in a magazine in 1890.

78145.e: Werther wears a blue tailcoat with a yellow waistcoat, writes letters and suffers from his unhappy love for Lotte.

78146.q: Which novella do these pictures mean?

78149.m: Thomas Mann's novel about Hans Castorp is set in a sanatorium in Davos.

78150.m: Thomas Mann won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929 mainly for his first novel about a Lübeck family.

78151.q: Which Romantic story do these emojis show?
78151.e: A young man sells his shadow to a mysterious gentleman in a grey coat and receives in return a purse that is never empty.
78151.m: Adelbert von Chamisso published the story of the man without a shadow in 1814.

78152.m: The story appeared in 1816 in E. T. A. Hoffmann's collection “Night Pieces”.

78153.e: A black spider and the devil: after a pact with the devil a plague of spiders strikes the village, until the spider is locked inside a wooden post.

78154.q: Which novel by Jeremias Gotthelf do these pictures mean?
78154.e: A young farmhand learns to be thrifty and hard-working and rises to become a capable head farmhand with savings.
78154.m: The novel about a farmhand's rise in the Emmental came out in 1841.

78155.q: Which novella by Gottfried Keller do these emojis show?

78157.q: Which novel by Max Frisch do these emojis show?

78157.m: The novel begins with the sentence “I'm not Stiller!”.

78158.q: Which story by Peter Bichsel do these pictures mean?
78158.e: A lonely old man gives all things new names, for example he calls the bed “picture”, until nobody understands him any more.
78158.m: Peter Bichsel's story about the old man appeared in 1969 in the book “Stories for Children”.

78159.q: Which story by Robert Walser do these emojis show?
78159.e: A writer in a hat walks through woods and villages and describes everything he comes across on the way.
78159.m: Robert Walser published the story in 1917.

78160.q: Which novel by Charles Ferdinand Ramuz do these pictures mean?
78160.e: A rockfall buries an alpine pasture with huts and animals; the herdsman Antoine survives for weeks under the rocks and comes back.

78161.q: Which play by Friedrich Schiller do these emojis show?
78161.e: Two queens and chains: Mary, Queen of Scots, is a prisoner in England and meets Queen Elizabeth in the park.
78161.m: Friedrich Schiller's play about the two queens was first performed in Weimar in 1800.

78162.q: Which comedy by Heinrich von Kleist do these pictures mean?
78162.e: A broken jug and a lying judge: village judge Adam is supposed to find out who broke the jug, and he did it himself.
78162.m: In Kleist's comedy from 1808 a judge tries to cover up his own guilt.

78163.q: Which play by Shakespeare do these emojis show?

78163.m: The play about the magician Prospero is considered one of the last that Shakespeare wrote on his own.

78164.q: Which comedy by Molière do these pictures mean?
78164.e: A man lies in bed, thinks he is seriously ill and lets doctors fleece him, although there is nothing wrong with him.
78164.m: Molière wrote the comedy about Argan in 1673 as his last play.

78165.q: Which comedy do these emojis show?
78165.e: A rich man hides a cash box in the garden and flies into a rage when it disappears: Harpagon is the miser of all misers.
78165.m: The main character Harpagon from Molière's comedy of 1668 is the classic example of a miser.

78166.q: Which Greek tragedy do these pictures mean?
78166.e: A young woman wants to bury her dead brother against King Creon's ban and follows her conscience instead of the law.
78166.m: Sophocles' tragedy about Creon's niece was performed in Athens around 442 BC.

78167.q: Which play by Gerhart Hauptmann do these emojis show?
78167.e: Poor home workers at the loom are exploited by a rich factory owner and rise up against him.
78167.m: Gerhart Hauptmann's play about the Silesian uprising of 1844 came out in 1892.

78168.q: Which play by Henrik Ibsen do these pictures mean?

78168.m: Henrik Ibsen's verse drama came out in 1867, and Edvard Grieg wrote famous incidental music for it.

78169.q: Which comedy do these emojis show?
78169.e: A poor shoemaker buys an officer's uniform, uses it to occupy a town hall and has the town's cash handed over to him.
78169.m: Carl Zuckmayer's play of 1931 is based on a real incident from 1906.

78170.q: Which classic film do these emojis mean?
78170.e: A ship, an iceberg, a tragic love story and the musicians who keep playing to the end: the film tells the story of the Titanic in 1912.
78170.m: James Cameron's film about the sinking of the luxury liner won eleven Oscars in 1998.

78171.q: Which film do these emojis show?
78171.e: On an island dinosaurs are bred from ancient DNA, and visitors drive through the park in off-road vehicles.
78171.m: Steven Spielberg's dinosaur film came out in cinemas in 1993.

78172.q: Which film by Steven Spielberg do these pictures mean?
a: Close Encounters of the Third Kind
78172.e: An alien flies past the moon with a boy on a bike and wants to phone home.
78172.m: In the 1982 film the creature from space wants to “phone home”.

78173.q: Which film do these emojis show?
78173.e: A car becomes a time machine, lightning strikes the town hall clock, and Marty McFly rides a skateboard in the past.
78173.m: In the 1985 film a converted DeLorean serves as a time machine.

78174.q: Which classic film from 1942 do these pictures mean?
78174.e: In Rick's Café, Sam plays “As Time Goes By” on the piano, and at the end a plane takes off in the fog.
78174.m: Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman play the leading roles in the film about Rick's Café in Morocco.

78175.q: Which classic film do these emojis show?
78175.e: A giant ape climbs a skyscraper in New York holding a woman in his hand and is circled by aeroplanes.
78175.m: The film with the giant ape came out in cinemas in 1933 and ends on the Empire State Building.

78176.q: Which film by Charlie Chaplin do these pictures mean?
78176.e: The Tramp with his bowler hat and big shoes works on a factory assembly line and gets caught between huge cogs.
78176.m: Charlie Chaplin's 1936 film criticises assembly-line work.

78177.q: Which silent film do these emojis show?
78177.e: A huge city of the future, factories in the underworld and a machine-man that looks like the young Maria.
78177.m: Fritz Lang's silent film of 1927 is part of UNESCO's Memory of the World.

78178.q: Which opera by Mozart do these emojis show?
78178.e: Belmonte wants to free his beloved Konstanze from the palace of a pasha and tries to escape at night with a ladder.
78178.m: Mozart's opera about Konstanze's rescue was first performed in Vienna in 1782.

78179.q: Which opera by Giuseppe Verdi do these pictures mean?

78179.m: Verdi's opera about the court jester was first performed in Venice in 1851.

78180.q: Which opera do these emojis show?
